learn.title: Superlatives
learn.html:
Use a superlative to say that one thing is number one in a group: the cheapest, the most expensive. Always use the before it.

AdjectiveRuleSuperlative
cheap, small, quietshort word: the + adjective + -estthe cheapest
nice, largeends in -e: + -stthe nicest
big, hotone vowel + one consonant: double itthe biggest
noisy, easyends in -y: change y to i + -estthe noisiest
expensive, comfortablelong word: the most + adjectivethe most expensive
good, bad, farirregularthe best, the worst, the farthest
  • After a superlative we use in + a place or group (in the building, in the city) or of + a number or a plural (of the three, of all).
  • Example: This is the biggest room in the house.

watch.wrong: It is the most cheap apartment.
This is the biggest room of the house.
watch.right: This is the biggest room in the house.
watch.why: Use in with a place; use of with a number or a plural (of the three).

watch.wrong: It is the most better area.
watch.why: Good has an irregular superlative: the best.

learn.title: Time clauses with before, after and when
learn.html:
A time clause starts with before, after or when. It says when something happens in relation to another action.

WordMeaningExample
beforethe first action comes secondBefore I sign the lease, I read every page.
afterthe first action comes firstAfter we moved in, we bought a table.
whenat the same time or right afterWhen I get home, I take off my shoes.
  • Both parts of the sentence use the same tense: present for habits (I always check...) or simple past for finished actions (I paid... I moved...).
  • If the time clause comes first, we put a comma: After I move in, I clean the kitchen. If it comes second, no comma: I clean the kitchen after I move in.
  • After before / after / when, use a subject + verb: before I sign. Do not use will in the time clause.

watch.wrong: Before I will sign the lease, I read it.
watch.right: Before I sign the lease, I read it.
watch.why: Do not use will in the time clause; use the simple present.

watch.wrong: After she moved in, she buys a lamp.
watch.right: After she moved in, she bought a lamp.
watch.why: Keep the same tense in both parts: past with past.

watch.wrong: After to finish work, I go home.
watch.right: After I finish work, I go home.
watch.why: After + subject + verb (or After finishing work).

watch.wrong: When I arrive home I cook dinner
watch.right: When I arrive home, I cook dinner.
watch.why: Put a comma after a time clause at the beginning of the sentence.

learn.title: Present real conditional: if + present, present
learn.html:
Use if + simple present, simple present to talk about things that are always true or usually happen. The if part is the condition; the other part is the result.

Condition (if + present)Result (present)
If you pay late,you pay a fine.
If it is hot,I open the windows.
If the heater doesn't work,I call the landlord.
Do you call the landlordif something breaks?
  • Both verbs are in the simple present: If I feel cold, I turn on the heater.
  • With a comma when if comes first; no comma when it comes second.
  • If is almost the same as when here: If / When the rent goes up, we look for a new place.
  • Do not use will after if in this structure.

watch.wrong: If you will pay late, you get a fine.
watch.right: If you pay late, you get a fine.
watch.why: No will after if; use the simple present.

watch.wrong: If the heater doesn't works, I call the landlord.
watch.right: If the heater doesn't work, I call the landlord.
watch.why: After doesn't, use the base form of the verb.

watch.wrong: If I am cold, I am turning on the heater.
watch.right: If I am cold, I turn on the heater.
watch.why: For habits and general results, use the simple present, not the continuous.

watch.wrong: If you don't pay the rent, you not keep the apartment.
watch.right: If you don't pay the rent, you don't keep the apartment.
watch.why: Make the result negative with don't / doesn't.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• Is the apartment still available? — the first question when you call.
  • How much is the rent? / How much is the deposit? — asking about money.
  • Are the utilities included in the rent? — asking what you pay.
  • Can I have a pet? — It depends on the landlord. — asking and answering about rules.
  • When can I move in? — asking about the date.
  • What's the neighborhood like? — asking about the area.
  • The best thing about it is the light. / The biggest problem is the noise. — evaluating a place.
  • I'll think about it and call you tomorrow. — a polite way to wait before you decide.

reading.title: Choosing a Place to Live
reading.intro: Read about Marta's apartment search and answer.
paragraphs: Finding a new home is exciting, but it can also be stressful. Before you sign anything, you need to think about what matters most to you. For some people, the most important thing is the price. For others, it is the location or the size of the place.

Marta is looking for an apartment in Guadalajara. She works downtown, so she wants to live near a metro station. When she compared three apartments, she made a list. The first one was the cheapest, but it was also the smallest and the noisiest. The second was the biggest, with two bedrooms and a balcony, but it was the farthest from her office. The third one was the most expensive, and it was the closest to the metro.

Marta visited each place twice: once in the morning and once at night. "When you visit only once, you can miss problems," she says. At night she found out that the street near the cheapest apartment was very loud. In the morning she checked the water and the windows. After she talked to the neighbors, she learned that the building with the balcony had a problem with the elevator.

Her cousin Luis gave her some advice. "If you pay more for a good location, you spend less on transportation," he said. "If the apartment is far from work, you lose time every day." He also told her to read the lease carefully. If you break the lease, you usually lose your deposit. Before she signed, Marta asked about the rent, the deposit and the utilities.

In the end, Marta chose the second apartment. It was not the closest, but the landlord agreed to fix the elevator and lower the rent a little. After she moved in, she bought a bicycle. Now she rides to the metro station in ten minutes. "It was the best decision," she says, "because I took my time."

a choice you make after you think about something

lines.text: Good morning. Welcome. Are you here to see the apartment on Pine Street?
Yes. I'm Ana, and this is my brother Pablo. He is going to share the apartment with me.
Nice to meet you. It's on the third floor, and it's the quietest apartment in the building.
It's six thousand five hundred pesos a month. Water is included, but you pay for electricity and internet.

Can we have a pet? I have a small cat.
Usually no. But if you ask the landlord, he sometimes says yes for small pets.
The kitchen is the biggest room! Is the stove new?
Yes, they changed it last month. Before you decide, please check the bedrooms too.
After you sign the lease and pay the deposit, you can move in on the first of the month.
Great. We'll talk about it tonight and call you tomorrow.
